title: It's Not Done Yet: Another DOJ Indictment!
subtitle: The Done ADHD case isn't over yet.
body_html:
This newsletter began covering (what I believed to be) unfair allegations about the behavior of Cerebral. But we can all see that there was some really untoward activity when it came to the prescribing of stimulant medications for ADHD. It turns out that the company, Done, at the heart of some of the most inappropriate prescribing, is also the most ironically named company in healthcare. Both the CEO and the chief medical officer were indicted, convicted, and are awaiting sentencing. This is a provider-specific article. There are learnings here. My prior writing on Done is available here.

However, the Department of Justice is in no way done with the prosecution of those involved, because, for reasons that make little sense to me, individuals behind the entity previously known as Done continued to operate and continued to prescribe stimulant medications.

A new indictment was dropped today. The DOJ did not mince words. I’m gonna do an annotated read for us all.

Adderall.

“As alleged, Done Global used lies and deceit to carry out a sophisticated and wide-ranging telehealth fraud scheme, obtaining over $100 million in the process,” said Acting Assistant Attorney General Matthew R. Galeotti of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “From feeding addiction to stealing public funds, rampant health care fraud victimizes our citizens and must be stopped. The Criminal Division will not hesitate to hold health care companies that defraud Americans accountable for their crimes.”

Done had rebranded and—despite a conviction of two officers!—rebranded to “Mindful,” and kept prescribing Speed for money.

Chutzpah does not begin to cover it. Mindful of what, I ask rhetorically. The DOJ press release is REALLY long, I’ll note:

Done Global betrayed the public trust by allegedly exploiting a subscription-based program

You know, drug dealing…which was and is a crime. The prescribing ability doesn’t make it not drug dealing. The medical care that accompanies it makes it legal. It’s like getting stabbed is assault unless the surgeon has a reason to cut you, that is, with informed consent and in the interest of the patient…

to flood the country with Adderall,

And did they ever. I spoke about it here.

a powerful and highly regulated controlled substance,” said Assistant Administrator Cheri Oz of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Diversion Control Division. “By distributing over 40 million Adderall pills for non-legitimate medical purposes, they prioritized profit over patient safety and public health.

40,000,000 pills.💊. Even the emoji for pills is an Adderall capsule.

Controlled substances are not commodities to be marketed through memberships — they are medications that require careful oversight to prevent misuse and diversion.

Yes, they are. Good Citizens knew this, and followed the rules. Done cashed in 40,000,000 times…and kept going after?!?

DEA remains steadfast in its commitment to hold registrants accountable.”

I mean, I wish this were more true—the DEA has even more cases to catch up on…*cough* sorry. We continue:

“Yesterday, we charged defendants with exploiting telehealth to provide unfettered access to over 40 million Adderall pills. Instead of leveraging technology to improve patient access to care and enhance communications,

This is, I suspect, a sly nod to the actually good work done at places like Cerebral. They may have broken some rules re: marketing, but there were non-prosecution agreements there.

Done Global saw it as a way to boost profit. We will vigorously pursue companies that engage in this kind of fraud and put patients at risk,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California.

Will you now? Are there others? *cough* Sorry.

“Prescribing controlled substances without proper medical oversight, as alleged, endangers patients and erodes trust in our health care system,”

As alleged and proved in another case, already concluded with a conviction.

said Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Christian J. Schrank of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG). “Running a sham operation to exploit federal programs and funnel taxpayer dollars into unlawful stimulant distribution is a blatant abuse.

Unless it’s a health plan, in which case we will let it slide—as UHG did 7 days ago.

HHS-OIG will continue to work with our law enforcement partners to expose and dismantle schemes that threaten public safety and defraud the American people.”

Please, do that.

“IRS Criminal Investigation special agents are specially equipped to follow the complex financial trail left by criminals, and we are dedicated to holding those accountable for crimes committed,” said Special Agent in Charge Harry T. Chavis of IRS Criminal Investigation New York

So this case will be about the books. Thanks DOJ! Tax fraud is a real crime, and it is easy to prove if you have already completed discovery in the first case.

“This was a brazen scheme of staggering proportions while also putting individual lives at risk.

Usually, I argue against adjectives, but it's hard to call this out without calling it brazen. It’s the definition of brazen.

Yesterday’s indictment sends a clear message that we remain vigilant and will vigorously pursue those who attempt to enrich themselves through fraudulent means.”

Please, do.

According to court documents, Done Global Inc., a California company, allegedly identified itself as a “digital health company,” which operated on a subscription-based model where individuals paid a monthly fee. Done Global advertised that it provided online diagnosis, treatment, and refills of medication for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). As alleged, Done Global and Mindful Mental Wellness P.A. (MMW), a Florida company,

Did I mention I hate the term wellness?

allegedly conspired with others to provide easy access to over 40 million pills of Adderall and other stimulants in exchange for payment of the monthly subscription fee. The indictment alleges that the conspiracy’s purpose was for the defendants to unlawfully enrich themselves by, among other things, instructing Done prescribers to prescribe Adderall and other stimulants without any legitimate medical purpose,

Tipped off by the word “wellness” in the name of the Florida medical group.

thereby increasing monthly subscription revenue and increasing the value of Done Global. Done Global allegedly arranged for the prescription of over 40 million pills of Adderall and other stimulants and obtained over $100 million in revenue.

That is, for a moment, a really low dollar value per pill, given they had to raise venture capital to get there. Pablo Escobar made $4 billion in top line. C’mon, Ruthia. Speaking of that scoundrel:

The founder and CEO of Done Global, Ruthia He, and Done Global’s former clinical president, David Brody, were previously convicted of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances, four counts of distribution of controlled substances and conspiracy to commit health care fraud. Ruthia He was also convicted of conspiracy to obstruct justice.

And now, more—and good. Every DEA license involved could be pulled. Let’s see some real consequences, DOJ. Oh, they also billed Medicare and Medicaid for this scam!? They preyed on the most vulnerable.

Done Global and MMW allegedly ordered Adderall and other stimulants for Done members, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and commercial insurers members, with whom they lacked a pre-existing practitioner-patient relationship, without an examination, and sometimes based solely on a short video or audio communication and limited patient intake documents, or without any video or audio communication at all.

Now, “how short” a video will matter. But this sets a standard. Other virtual care providers are watching closely.

Done Global, MMW, and others,

Wait—which others?

allegedly agreed to provide few, if any, medical treatment options besides prescribing Adderall and other stimulants. In some cases, Done members: (a) did not meet the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-V criteria for diagnosing ADHD;

Ok, so this clearly needs to be documented. Btw, note to DOJ: it’s DSM-5, not DSM-V.

(b) posed a risk of diversion; and (c) in the event such medications were necessary, were provided dosages, directions, combinations or quantities of medications beyond any legitimate medical purpose, and without following the usual course of professional practice for prescribing them.

Dosage matters—usual practice matters. AACAP has materials! Use them. Document the standard of care upon which your protocols are based.

By 2023, certain pharmacies allegedly refused to fill prescriptions written by prescribers retained by Done Health, a California Company that was affiliated with Done Global and purportedly owned by Brody. According to the indictment, Done Global incorporated MMW to circumvent the pharmacies that had blocked the filling of Done Global-affiliated prescriptions.

You know, to ensure ongoing wellness. And a risk of early death.

Done Global also allegedly conspired to alter, destroy, and conceal records after receiving a grand jury subpoena.

It’s not the crime, it’s the cover-up. And it’s a lot of cover-up, I’ll bet.

Done Global is charged with one count of conspiracy to illegally distribute Adderall,

One count? ONE COUNT?

four counts of illegal distribution of Adderall,

Only four counts is utterly bonkers.

conspiracy to commit health care fraud, and conspiracy to obstruct justice. If convicted, Done Global faces a maximum penalty for conspiracy and illegal distribution of Adderall of twice the gross profits or other proceeds; and twice the gain or twice the gross loss for conspiracy to commit health care fraud and obstruction.

Ok, a soapbox for a minute: this is not enough of a penalty. The interest on the ill-gotten gains renders this sort of half-measure meaningless. Twice the gross profits? These fines need to be so bad that no one wants to do anything like it ever again. The Perdue Sacklers are still very wealthy and paying all penalties out of interest on their ill-gotten gains. PRISON TIME, and financial ruin. With interest. Nothing else will even remotely discourage capital from flowing to nitwits like this in the future.

If convicted, MMW faces a maximum penalty for conspiracy to illegally distribute Adderall of twice the gross profits or other proceeds.

I’m bored already. What did everyone know and when did they know it?

The Fraud Section leads the Criminal Division’s efforts to combat health care fraud through the Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program.

I, for one, am glad to know the FBI still has a healthcare strike force, much less a program. Thank you, public servants. I mean that.

Since March 2007, this program, comprised of nine strike forces operating in 27 federal districts, has charged more than 5,800 defendants who collectively have billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $30 billion.

As a reminder, $30 billion is on the order of UHC's annual profits, but smaller. It’s a tiny amount of money in healthcare. Step it up, team. Step it up.

In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes.

Oh, thank goodness (maybe). I have limited faith that state medical boards will do much here—they move too slowly, especially in California.

More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

Thanks for the links!

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

This is true. And yet, given the “already convicted” founders, I doubt this will go that far south. But due process is due to all, even and especially the guilty.

The DOJ offers guidance on finding new providers, and, to be honest, it’s lacking:

Finding a New Provider

Patients receiving treatment at this practice may contact their insurance carrier for assistance in identifying a new provider for continued care. Individuals seeking access to a new primary care provider or other services can also find a provider through

https://findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov/

Yes, you insurance company will have plenty of in network stimulant prescribers handy…Except, I doubt they will. Honestly, much of this could be handled by primary care doctors, who are in able to manage the comorbidities common among ADHD sufferers, with appropriate supervision from psychiatrist colleagues.

Pro Tip: if you are going to take down 40,000,000 pills worth of anything, maybe create a collaborative care bonus payment model to handle the fallout. Many adults will still have ADHD, and will need treatment.

Crisis Support

Patients experiencing a mental health or substance use crisis can contact the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline for 24/7 support. Trained counselors provide confidential, judgment-free assistance.

This will similarly go well…oh, wait.

Additional Information

The Department of Justice and its law enforcement partners are working with public health and behavioral health partners to communicate where patients can find appropriate care and to alert them of potential risks associated with obtaining medications outside legal channels. Patients seeking further information on where to obtain care can refer to the CDC Health Advisory on a related action from June 13, 2024. Health Alert Network (HAN) - 00510 | Disrupted Access to Prescription Stimulant Medications Could Increase Risk of Injury and Overdose.

This was a dark chapter. Godspeed, DOJ. And best of luck to patients who needed care and got scammed—they are the real victims here.

There should be recompense for them, as well.
